property_summary: For any caller and uint value v, calling SetMinSum(v) on the correct contract always sets MinSum exactly to v (no reentrant change), whereas the buggy contract with a no-op nonReentrant_ modifier can be re-entered by a malicious fallback and cause MinSum to end up different after the call.

For any caller and any uint v, after calling SetMinSum(v) on the correct contract, MinSum equals v (no reentrant interference); the buggy variant with a no-op nonReentrant_ allows a reentrant attacker to change MinSum during the call so MinSum != v for some inputs.

For all inputs, calling SetMinSum(v) on the correct contract sets MinSum to v (no reentrant interference); the buggy variant with a removed lock allows a reentrant attacker (deployed helper) to reenter SetMinSum during the call and change MinSum so that after the call MinSum != v for some fuzzed v and attacker interactions.

For every attacker-supplied uint256 newMin and deposit amount, if a caller calls SetMinSum(newMin) on the correct contract while a malicious contract is registered as LogFile and attempts reentrancy during AddMessage, the correct contract's MinSum remains exactly newMin after the call (reentrancy is prevented); the mutant with a no-op nonReentrant_ allows the malicious LogFile to reenter and change MinSum so that MinSum != newMin for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any uint newMin, when SetMinSum(newMin) is invoked on the correct contract, it always returns (does not revert) and after the call MinSum == newMin; the mutant removing the nonReentrant_ lock can be re-entered by a malicious Log contract during the call to change MinSum so that after SetMinSum returns MinSum != newMin for some fuzzed newMin and attacker behaviour.

The reference contract's nonReentrant_ modifier prevents reentrant calls during SetMinSum (so calling SetMinSum reentrantly while it is executing is impossible), whereas removing the require allows a reentrant attacker to call SetMinSum again and change MinSum after the first call — breaking the invariant that a single external SetMinSum call cannot be re-entered to change MinSum mid-execution.

For any caller and any uint newVal, a single external call to SetMinSum(newVal) either completes without allowing reentrant SetMinSum calls (so MinSum equals newVal after the call); the mutant without the require can be reentered by a malicious recipient during the external call and cause MinSum to differ (the mutant can result in MinSum != newVal).

For any caller and any uint newVal, a single external call to SetMinSum(newVal) on the reference contract always returns MinSum == newVal (modifier blocks reentrant entries), whereas the mutant that removes the require(!locked_) can be reentered by a malicious log contract and end up with MinSum != newVal.

For any caller and any uint newVal and any adversarial Log contract, a single external call to SetMinSum(newVal) on the correct contract always leaves MinSum equal to newVal at completion (non-reentrancy enforced); the mutant removing the require(!locked_) can be reentered via the Log contract during the call and leave MinSum different from newVal.

For any caller and any uint newVal and any Log-like callee, a single external call to SetMinSum(newVal) on the correct contract always ends with MinSum == newVal (nonReentrant_ prevents any reentrant change), but removing the require allows a malicious Log fallback to reenter and change MinSum so MinSum may differ from newVal.

For any caller and any address argument, calling SetLogFile(...) on the correct contract sets LogFile to the provided address iff the contract is already initialized state is true only in the mutant — the reference allows setting the LogFile when intitalized is false (before Initialized is called); the mutant returns early when not initialized, so for inputs where initialized is false the stored LogFile differs between reference and mutant.

For any address X, calling SetLogFile(X) when the contract is not yet initialized must set LogFile to X (reference satisfies this for all inputs); the mutant inverts the check and leaves LogFile unchanged when not initialized, so there exist inputs where LogFile differs after SetLogFile.

For any address X, calling SetLogFile(X) on the reference when the contract is not yet initialized sets LogFile to X (the reference always assigns LogFile when intitalized==false), whereas the mutant returns early when not initialized and thus leaves LogFile unchanged for some X — so after SetLogFile(X) completes with intitalized==false the stored LogFile equals X in the reference but may differ in the mutant.
If the contract is not initialized, calling SetLogFile(addr) always sets LogFile to addr in the reference; the mutant instead no-ops when not initialized so LogFile may differ.

For any address x and when the contract is not yet initialized, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract always sets LogFile to x (the reference guarantees LogFile == x after the call); the mutant inverts the check and will not set LogFile when not initialized, violating this rule for some x.

Reference contract's nonReentrant_ modifier prevents re-entrancy into SetLogFile so calling SetLogFile (even when the provided address is a malicious contract that calls back) always returns without reentrant resets of LogFile; the mutated contract (which removed locked_ toggles) allows a re-entrant attacker to change C.LogFile during SetLogFile leading to a different final LogFile address than in the reference for some inputs.

After calling SetLogFile(attacker), the reference contract C always completes without allowing the called address to become the final LogFile via reentrancy (i.e., SetLogFile returns with LogFile equal to the address passed in), whereas the mutant that removes the reentrancy guard can be forced by a reentrant attacker to leave LogFile set to a different address.

For every address input A, calling SetLogFile(A) on the reference contract always completes and leaves LogFile equal to A; the mutant lacking the reentrancy guard can be made (via a reentrant attacker) to end with LogFile different from A for some A.

For any address A, calling SetLogFile(A) on the correct contract always returns successfully and leaves LogFile equal to A (i.e., address(c.LogFile()) == A); the mutant that removes the nonReentrant_ assignments can be re-entered by a malicious callee during SetLogFile and thus can end with LogFile not equal to A for some attacker addresses.

For any address A, calling SetLogFile(A) on the correct contract always returns (does not revert) and leaves LogFile equal to A; the mutant that removed the nonReentrant_ toggles can be re-entered by a malicious callee during SetLogFile so for some attacker addresses the final LogFile != A.

For any caller and address argument, calling SetLogFile(...) on the correct contract always succeeds the first time (sets LogFile to the provided address) while the buggy mutant permanently locks the reentrancy guard so a subsequent call to SetLogFile by any caller will revert; the test fuzzes a caller and target and checks that after one successful SetLogFile, a second SetLogFile call (possibly by different caller) still succeeds on the reference but may fail on the mutant.

After calling Initialized() the reference contract permanently sets intitalized to true (so the getter intitalized() returns true for any caller), whereas the mutant clears it to false, so there exist inputs where the getter returns false after the call.

After any call to Initialized() the reference contract sets the public flag intitalized to true (sticky), while the mutant sets it to false, so the property is: for all callers, calling Initialized() makes c.intitalized() return true; the mutant violates this for some caller.

For any caller, invoking Initialized() on the correct contract sets the public flag intitalized to true (the call succeeds and the getter returns true); the mutant that sets it to false will make that getter return false for some callers, so the universal property 'after calling Initialized(), c.intitalized() == true' holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant.

For any caller and any prior state, calling Initialized() on the correct contract makes the public flag intitalized become true (the call returns normally and the getter reports true); the mutant that sets intitalized = false breaks this by leaving the flag false after the call for some inputs.

For any caller address, calling Initialized() on the correct contract sets the public boolean intitalized to true (sticky); the mutant that sets intitalized = false causes that getter to be false after the call for some caller inputs.

Calling Initialized() from any caller always sets the contract's public bool intitalized to true in the reference (it becomes initialized and stays true), whereas the mutant that toggles it can leave it false for some call sequences (e.g., calling Initialized twice returns it to false).

After any single call sequence where Initialized() is invoked exactly once by any address, the reference contract's public bool intitalized is true (monotonic set-to-true), while the mutant that toggles it can leave intitalized false for some inputs (e.g., when it was initially false and the toggling implementation is used).

Invariant: calling Initialized() (from any single caller) makes C.intitalized() permanently true in the reference; the mutant that toggles can produce a call sequence (two calls by potentially different callers) that results in intitalized being false, so the property that "after two successive calls to Initialized() by possibly different callers the contract remains initialized (true)" is violated by the mutant.

Invariant: once Initialized() has been called an odd number of times, the reference contract's public bool intitalized is true and stays true for any further non-reverting calls; the mutant that toggles can make intitalized false for some call counts (e.g., when called twice), so there exists a sequence of calls (specifically two calls) and caller ordering that causes the mutant to violate the invariant while the reference preserves it.

Rule: Once any address has successfully called Initialized(), the public getter intitalized() is true thereafter (i.e., any subsequent call to Initialized() does not change it from true to false); the mutant toggling implementation can flip it back to false on a subsequent call, violating this permanence property.

For any caller and call, invoking Initialized() on the correct contract always sets the public bool intitalized to true (call returns without revert), whereas the mutant reverts if intitalized was already true, so there exist inputs where a second call will leave intitalized false after the attempted call (i.e., the call can fail and not set it).

Calling Initialized() on a fresh contract always results in c.intitalized() == true (reference sets the flag unconditionally), whereas the mutant reverts when already initialized and can leave the flag unchanged for some sequences of calls, so the property is: after a single successful Initialized() call by any address the public flag intitalized is true.

For any caller and any prior state, after a successful call to Initialized() the contract's public bool intitalized becomes true; the mutant reverts when intitalized is already true, allowing a scenario where a second call does not set it and thus violates this rule.

For any caller and any prior contract state, a successful call to Initialized() returns (does not revert) and leaves the public flag intitalized true; the mutant makes Initialized() revert when already initialized, so there exist call sequences where a (second) call reverts and leaves the flag unchanged, violating this rule.

For any single caller and any prior state, either the first call to Initialized() succeeds and sets c.intitalized() to true, or if Initialized() is already true then any attempt to call Initialized() will revert; the reference always allows a call that sets the flag true at least once (so there exists an admissible caller and call that results in c.intitalized()==true), whereas the mutant can make the second call revert and thus prevents a subsequent call from observing the flag transition — we state the rule as: after a single call to Initialized() from a fresh caller (one that has not previously invoked Initialized on this c instance) the public getter c.intitalized() is true.

For any caller, calling Initialized() on the reference contract always returns true (succeeds) and sets intitalized to true; the mutant's broken nonReentrant_ modifier causes subsequent calls to revert (locked_ stays true) so Initialized() can fail for some call ordering, breaking this property.

For any caller address, calling Initialized() on a fresh contract instance should always succeed (set intitalized to true and return normally); the mutant that never resets locked_ can cause Initialized() to revert when invoked after any nonReentrant_ call that left locked_ true, violating this invariant for some sequences of calls.

For any caller and any calldata, calling Initialized() on a fresh C instance always succeeds (sets intitalized to true and does not revert); the mutant that fails to reset locked_ can leave locked_ true after any nonReentrant_ call, causing subsequent Initialized() calls to revert and thus violate this rule for some input sequences.

For any caller and any prior nonReentrant_ call that completes successfully, calling Initialized() on the reference C always succeeds (sets intitalized to true and does not revert); the mutant that never resets locked_ can leave locked_ == true causing Initialized() to revert for some sequences, violating this rule.

For any caller and any prior successful nonReentrant_ protected call, calling Initialized() on the correct contract always succeeds (sets intitalized to true and does not revert); the mutant that never resets locked_ can leave locked_ == true after a prior nonReentrant_ call, causing Initialized() to revert for some input sequences.

After any Put(msg.value, _lockTime) by an account, the resulting acc.unlockTime in the correct contract is always at least block.timestamp + _lockTime (i.e., unlockTime >= now + _lockTime); the mutant uses msg.value instead of _lockTime so for some inputs unlockTime < now + _lockTime and thus violates this rule.

For any call to Put by an account sending value v and specifying lock time t, the reference contract ensures the account's unlockTime after Put is at least block.timestamp + t; the mutant (which uses msg.value instead of t) can produce unlockTime < block.timestamp + t for some fuzzed (v,t).

For any caller and inputs, after Put(...) in the reference contract the stored unlockTime is equal to max(previous unlockTime, block.timestamp + _lockTime); the mutant erroneously uses msg.value so when msg.value < _lockTime the mutant can leave unlockTime smaller than block.timestamp + _lockTime.

For any caller, after calling Put(_lockTime) with value v the reference sets acc.unlockTime to at least its previous value and to at least block.timestamp + min(_lockTime, type(uint).max) (i.e. it uses the provided _lockTime when increasing unlockTime); the mutant uses msg.value instead of _lockTime so when v < _lockTime the mutant can leave unlockTime smaller than block.timestamp + _lockTime, violating this rule.

For any caller, after calling Put(_lockTime) with value v the reference contract ensures the caller's unlockTime >= block.timestamp + _lockTime (it uses the provided _lockTime to extend the unlock), whereas the mutant uses msg.value instead and can leave unlockTime < block.timestamp + _lockTime when v < _lockTime.

For any caller and any msg.value, calling Put increases the caller's recorded balance by exactly msg.value (i.e., new balance == old balance + msg.value); the mutant overwrites instead of adds and thus violates this when caller had a pre-existing balance and msg.value>0.

For any caller and any positive deposit value, calling Put increases that caller's recorded balance by exactly the call's msg.value (i.e., newBalance == oldBalance + msg.value); the mutant overwrites balance with msg.value and thus violates this when the caller already had a non-zero balance and then calls Put with a positive msg.value.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after calling Put the stored balance equals the previous stored balance plus msg.value (i.e., Put accumulates deposits rather than overwriting); the mutant that assigns acc.balance = msg.value breaks this when the caller already has a non-zero balance and makes another deposit.

For any caller and any two sequential deposits (first amount a1, then a2) into the same account, the reference contract ensures the stored balance after the second deposit equals previousBalance + a2 (i.e. it accumulates deposits), whereas the mutant that assigns acc.balance = msg.value breaks this when the first deposit is non-zero and the second deposit occurs (it resets balance to the second deposit instead of adding).
